items.author: EdPiotrowskiWPDE
items.text:
The last two days in Glacier National Park with Cindy and our dear friends, Matt and Carrie Harris, were nothing short of amazing. Connecting with nature and taking in the beauty of God's incredible creation was awe inspiring and so good for the mind and soul. I thought about and talked to Mom while we were out there, and in the quiet moments surrounded by those mountains, I felt especially close to her. That feeling was a precious gift and a blessing I’ll carry with me.

We covered 22 miles of rugged trails in just two days. Our bodies are sore and tired, but our hearts are overflowing with gratitude, joy, and memories we’ll cherish for a long time.

We even had a close encounter with a grizzly! You can see the video above this post. Many of you have asked whether we had bear spray…we did. It was attached to the front of my backpack, right on my chest.

Today, we’re taking a quiet day to rest, before heading home early Monday morning.

items.author: TornadoChasing
items.text:
STRONG TORNADO 🌪 AREA TOMORROW‼

Its been awhile since we've seen a strong (ef-2) tornado area highlighted by the SPC but tomorrow the potential exists across eastern #Nebraska, including the #Omaha area into western #Iowa.

This is a bit of a tricky setup. We're heading into fall and wind shear gets increasingly strong, but there are some thermodynamic uncertainties that lower confidence a bit. Additionally, a very moist, high PWAT airmass along with strong frontal forcing gives a stronger signal for clustered heavy rain makers above all.

Still, with very strong low level shear in place, all it takes is a touch more instability and a discrete storm mode that lasts more than 45 minutes to get strong rotation and therefore, strong tornado potential going. Its an evolving situation to watch!

Regardless of what happens tornado wise, damaging winds and very large (2+") hail will also be possible!

An isolated severe thunderstorm threat is targeting eastern Nebraska and Iowa tomorrow!

A strong weather disturbance pushing out of the Rockies will track across the northern Plains Monday night, bringing strengthening winds to the Upper Midwest. While these winds will create an environment supportive of severe storms, there is still significant uncertainty regarding how much storm fuel will actually be available.

Widespread morning rain and elevated thunderstorms are expected to track across the region early in the day, which may leave the atmosphere too cool and stable for robust severe storms to form later on. If the atmosphere can recover and warm up along a stalled front, an isolated severe thunderstorm or a small, organized cluster could develop, with all hazards being possible.

items.author: JeffBerardelli
items.text:
It’s astonishing to see this, even though we saw it coming months ago. White = 10°F + above normal in the El Niño regions. It’s a huge area.
In the air, a regional warming of 10° is no big deal. But in the ocean it’s immense! Think about how hard it is/ how long it takes to cool/ heat your pool. Now multiply that by a trillion. Warming like this truly has no precedent in the historical record, and thus the impacts are unprecedented. From an almost non-existent Atlantic #hurricane season to a super-charged Pacific season. And coming this winter a supercharged subtropical jet stream with heavy rain storms and severe weather across the US South - #Florida, the Gulf Coast and probably flooding rains in California. And those are just the obvious impacts. Stay tuned! #ElNino @topfans

WE HAD A CLOSE ENCOUNTER WITH A GRIZZLY BEAR! 🐻

Matt & Carrie Harris and Cindy & I were hiking the Highline Trail in Glacier National Park on Saturday when we spotted a grizzly in the distance, on the trail and heading our way. I took the first zoomed-in video while he was still about 200 yards away.

If you’ve hiked the Highline, you know some stretches are so narrow there’s nowhere to step aside. So we backtracked a bit then climbed the rocks to higher a perch above the trail to give him plenty of room to pass. In the second video, Matt was still climbing higher as the bear walked by just below us!

We stood quietly together with bear spray in hand, hoping he’d keep going rather than come up toward us. Thankfully, he went on his merry way. We’re grateful everyone is safe, and we have one wild story to tell!

That was our first encounter with a grizzly bear. Honestly, it was a heart-pounding moment!

items.author: MeteorologistChristopherNunley
items.text:
DOES THIS PATTERN LOOK A LITTLE LIKE EL NIÑO? IT DOES🌧️take a look at the precipitation pattern expected across the Lower-48 over the next couple of weeks. There are definitely some characteristics that resemble the type of pattern we often associate with El Niño.

The Climate Prediction Center’s 6-10 day outlook, covering September 17-21, favors above-normal precipitation across a large part of the Southwest, Rockies and Southern Plains. Arizona, New Mexico, Utah, Colorado, Nevada, southern California, Texas, Oklahoma and Kansas are among the areas leaning wetter than normal. This is likely due to a tropical moisture transport responsible for the wetter signal across much of the West with the highest probabilities  centered over the Southwest and nearby areas. There is also a wetter signal extending from parts of the Mississippi and Ohio valleys toward the Mid-Atlantic and Northeast, while the Northern Plains and Upper Midwest lean drier. The Pacific Northwest, particularly Washington also initially leans drier. A similar signal continues with the 8-14 day outlook for September 19-25.

Does that mean every part of this pattern is being caused by El Niño? No! Individual troughs, ridges, tropical systems and shorter-term atmospheric variability are still driving the day-to-day weather. But the broader setup is interesting as we have a strengthening El Niño in the tropical Pacific, an active Eastern and Central Pacific, and an increasingly noticeable pipeline of tropical-subtropical moisture into parts of the western and southern United States. That combination - enhanced southern-tier-Pacific moisture with an increasingly active storm track across portions of the southern and western U.S. - certainly has an El Niño flavor to it. Also, remember, we're only in September. The classic El Niño influence on the U.S. becomes considerably more important as we move toward late fall and winter🌧️

Yesterday at the 9/11 Commemoration at OCC Road House, I had the privilege of hearing Greg Mertz, a retired United States Secret Service agent, share his remarkable story from September 11, 2001.

Greg was with President George W. Bush in Florida that morning and walked us through the events almost minute by minute — the uncertainty, the split-second decisions, and the responsibility of protecting the President as our country came under attack.

But his service didn’t end there. Shortly afterward, Greg was sent to Ground Zero, where he spent almost two weeks assisting with the heartbreaking search and recovery effort.

Listening to him describe what he witnessed, the people he encountered, and the weight carried by everyone working at Ground Zero was incredibly moving. You could hear the emotion in his voice even 25 years later.

Greg, thank you for your service to our country, for what you did on that terrible day and in the days that followed, and for continuing to share your story so future generations understand what happened and why we must never forget.

I’m also grateful that several members of our team were there with me to share in such a meaningful day of remembrance and reflection.

We honor the innocent lives we lost, the heroes who ran toward danger, and all those whose lives were forever changed by September 11.

🇺🇸 Never Forget.

items.author: secretsofuniverse
items.text:
🌑 Before this, everything humans had ever built stayed on or near Earth. Every tool, every machine, every object we'd ever made in our entire history had never touched another world. Then a Soviet probe slammed into the Moon at nearly 11,000 kilometres per hour, and that was no longer true.

On September 13, 1959, the Soviet Union's Luna 2 became the first human-made object to reach the surface of another celestial body. It wasn't a gentle landing. Luna 2 had no brakes, no thrusters, no way to slow down. It was designed to crash, and it did, hitting the Moon at about 3 kilometres per second between two lunar plains called Mare Imbrium and Mare Serenitatis.

The probe carried simple instruments, and in its brief flight it made a genuine discovery: the Moon has essentially no magnetic field and no radiation belts like Earth's. Just before impact, it scattered small metal pennants stamped with the Soviet coat of arms and the date, deliberately seeding the Moon with markers of who had gotten there first.

The timing was pointed. Soviet Premier Nikita Khrushchev was about to visit the United States, and he handed President Eisenhower a replica of the pennant as a gift. The message was hard to miss. This was the Cold War playing out 380,000 kilometres from Earth.

items.author: secretsofuniverse
items.text:
🌋 Venus is not a dead world after all.

Scientists have found the first direct geological evidence of recent volcanic activity on the surface of Venus.

The clue was hiding in radar images taken more than 30 years ago by NASA’s Magellan spacecraft.

Magellan could see through Venus’ thick clouds using radar, mapping a surface we cannot observe directly in visible light.

When researchers compared two images from 1991, they noticed something had changed near Maat Mons, one of the planet’s largest volcanoes.

A volcanic vent that first covered about 2.2 square kilometers had grown and changed shape within eight months.

In the later image, the vent appeared larger, misshapen and filled to the rim, possibly by a fresh lava lake.

The team modeled different explanations, including the effect of viewing the same feature from different angles.

But the best match was an eruption.

That matters because Venus and Earth are nearly the same size, yet they evolved into completely different worlds.

If Venus is volcanically active today, its interior is still shaping the planet’s surface, atmosphere and long-term evolution.

A planet once thought to be geologically quiet may still be burning from within.

📄 RESEARCH PAPER
📌 Herrick et al., “Surface changes observed on a Venusian volcano during the Magellan mission”, Science (2023)

RECORD QUIET IN THE TROPICS

We’re approaching the middle of September, traditionally the heart of hurricane season, and the Atlantic has been remarkably quiet.

In fact, we’re seeing a stretch of tropical inactivity that is approaching record territory for this point in the season.

That doesn’t mean hurricane season is over. We still have plenty of time left, and things can change quickly. But considering how active many forecasts expected this season to be, the lack of activity during the climatological peak is certainly noteworthy.

Sometimes the biggest weather story is what isn’t happening.

🧬 GLP-1 drugs may do more than trigger insulin — they may rewire how pancreatic cells behave.

GLP-1 medicines, including drugs used for type 2 diabetes and obesity, are known for helping pancreatic beta cells release insulin.

But scientists have been trying to understand their longer-lasting effects.

In a new study, researchers found that prolonged GLP-1 exposure activates a molecular switch inside beta cells.

The key protein is Med14, part of the cell’s gene-control machinery. When Med14 was phosphorylated at one specific site, it helped turn on broad genetic programs linked to insulin secretion, cell survival, metabolism, protein processing, and stress resistance.

In cell experiments, long-term exposure affected more than 1,000 genes.

The team also confirmed the pathway in mouse pancreatic islet cells.

This does not prove every long-term GLP-1 effect in humans. But it reveals how these drugs may reshape beta-cell biology beyond their immediate insulin effect.

📃 RESEARCH PAPER
📌 Van de Velde et al., “Med14 phosphorylation shapes genomic response to GLP-1 agonists”, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (2026)

🌙 The most famous line in the speech nearly went unheard. Right before it, Kennedy landed a joke about a football rivalry that got such a big laugh from the crowd that the iconic words almost got buried under it. "We choose to go to the Moon in this decade and do the other things, not because they are easy, but because they are hard."

On September 12, 1962, President John F. Kennedy stood before around 40,000 people in the sweltering heat of Rice Stadium in Houston, Texas, and made the case for sending Americans to the Moon. At the time, this was an almost outrageous promise. The United States had barely managed to put a man in orbit. The technology to reach the Moon did not exist yet.

What makes the speech remarkable is how honestly it faced that gap. Kennedy wasn't promising something easy. He was asking the country to commit to something genuinely hard, with no guarantee it would work, and to fund it, and to see it through.

A May 1961 poll had shown only 42 percent of Americans backed the idea. The speech was meant to change that. Seven years later, Apollo 11 landed. After Neil Armstrong stepped onto the surface, someone left flowers at Kennedy's grave with a note: "Mr. President, the Eagle has landed."

🧬 A cannabis-linked receptor may reveal a new way to slow breast cancer spread — but this is still early science.

Researchers focused on CB2R, a cannabinoid receptor involved in immune and inflammatory signaling.

Using human and mouse breast cancer organoids, they found that a brief, ultra-low-dose cannabinoid treatment could push tumor cells into a more stable, less aggressive identity.

The treated cells showed reduced invasiveness, weaker self-renewal, and lower tumor-starting ability.

In mouse experiments, these effects persisted after transplantation. Tumors formed later, grew more slowly, and showed less aggressive features.

The treatment also appeared to make some breast cancer cells more responsive to tamoxifen, a common hormone therapy.

This does not mean cannabis treats breast cancer. It does not support self-medicating with THC.

Instead, it points to CB2R as a possible future target for therapies that make cancer cells less plastic and harder to spread.

📃 RESEARCH PAPER
📌 Martínez-Illescas et al., “Transient CB2R modulation durably restricts breast cancer plasticity by stabilizing a luminal like cell identity”, Communications Biology (2026)

🌊 Saturn’s icy moon Enceladus now has the full chemical toolkit for life as we know it.

Scientists have confirmed phosphorus in tiny ice grains blasted from Enceladus’s hidden ocean into space.

That matters because phosphorus was the last major missing element in the famous CHNOPS list: carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, phosphorus and sulfur.

Together, these six elements are essential to life on Earth.

They help build DNA, RNA, proteins, cell membranes and the energy-carrying molecules that keep living cells running.

Enceladus already had a strong case for habitability.

NASA’s Cassini spacecraft found that the moon has a global ocean beneath its icy shell, organic compounds in its plume, salts, and signs of hydrothermal chemistry on the ocean floor.

Now, the detection of sodium phosphates in ocean-derived ice grains makes the case even stronger.

The study also suggests that phosphate may be at least 100 times more concentrated in Enceladus’s plume-forming ocean waters than in Earth’s oceans.

This does not mean life has been found.

But it means Enceladus has liquid water, possible energy sources and the major chemical ingredients life needs.

A tiny moon around Saturn has become one of the most promising places to search for life beyond Earth.

📄 RESEARCH PAPER
📌 Postberg et al., “Detection of phosphates originating from Enceladus’s ocean”, Nature (2023)

🦴 Calcium and vitamin D are essential for bones — but supplements may not prevent fractures for most older adults.

Researchers reviewed 69 randomized clinical trials involving 153,902 adults, comparing calcium, vitamin D, both together, placebo, or no treatment.

The result was surprisingly modest. Across the evidence, supplements had little to no clinically meaningful effect on overall fractures, hip fractures, vertebral fractures, or falls.

That does not mean calcium and vitamin D are unimportant. Bones need them, and supplements can still matter for people with deficiency, very low intake, malabsorption, osteoporosis treatment plans, or medical advice from a doctor.

But for many generally healthy older adults, a pill alone is not a strong fracture-prevention strategy.

Bone protection is bigger than supplements: strength training, balance work, enough protein, fall-proofing the home, vision checks, and osteoporosis screening may matter more.

The takeaway is not “ignore bone health.” It is: don’t rely only on the bottle.

📃 RESEARCH PAPER
📌 Massé et al., “Calcium, vitamin D, or combined supplementation to prevent fractures and falls: systematic review and meta-analysis”, BMJ (2026)

🌊 Saturn’s “Death Star” moon may be hiding one of the youngest oceans in the Solar System.

The moon is Mimas, a small icy world only about 400 kilometers wide.

At first glance, Mimas looks almost dead. Its surface is heavily cratered, and its giant Herschel crater makes it look like the Death Star from Star Wars.

That is why this discovery surprised scientists.

Using data from NASA’s Cassini spacecraft, researchers studied tiny changes in Mimas’s orbit around Saturn.

Those changes are hard to explain if Mimas is frozen solid all the way through.

The best fit is a global ocean of liquid water beneath an icy shell about 20 to 30 kilometers thick.

Even stranger, the ocean appears to be extremely young.

Models suggest it may have formed only 5 to 15 million years ago, possibly because Saturn’s tides recently began heating Mimas’s interior.

That may explain why the surface still looks old and quiet.

The ocean has not existed long enough to crack the crust or produce Enceladus-like geysers.

Mimas was one of the last places scientists expected to find liquid water.

Now, it may be a hidden ocean world caught near the beginning of its life.

📄 RESEARCH PAPER
📌 Lainey et al., “A recently formed ocean inside Saturn’s moon Mimas”, Nature (2024)

🧬 Evolution may have a blind spot — and aging lives inside it.

A new review argues that many late-life diseases make more sense when seen through evolution.

Natural selection strongly favors traits that help survival and reproduction early in life. But once reproduction is mostly complete, its power weakens.

That creates a “selection shadow,” where harmful effects that appear late in life are not removed as efficiently.

Some genes may even be kept because they help in youth, despite raising disease risk later.

This could help explain why aging is linked to conditions such as cancer, heart disease, dementia, inflammation, and tissue decline.

The review does not say aging is simple or inevitable in only one way.

Instead, it suggests that long life exposes biological trade-offs that evolution optimized for earlier survival, not decades of healthy old age.

Understanding those trade-offs may help scientists target healthspan, not just lifespan.

📃 RESEARCH PAPER
📌 Dönertaş and Partridge, “Evolutionary genetics of ageing”, Nature Reviews Genetics (2026)

🥤 Researchers analyzed long-term diet and health data from 112,284 U.S. adults in the Nurses’ Health Study and Health Professionals Follow-up Study.

Over more than 3.2 million person-years of follow-up, 278 people developed gastric cancer.

Compared with people who drank fewer than one sugar-sweetened beverage per month, daily consumers had a 2.45-fold higher risk of developing stomach cancer.

These drinks included regular sodas, punch, lemonade, and sports drinks.

Higher fructose intake was also linked to greater gastric cancer risk, while artificially sweetened beverages were not clearly linked.

But this was observational research. It cannot prove sugary drinks directly caused cancer, and factors such as H. pylori infection, weight, diet, and lifestyle may also matter.

Still, cutting back on sugary drinks remains a low-risk choice for long-term health.

📃 RESEARCH PAPER
📌 Gweon et al., “Association between sugar-sweetened and artificially sweetened beverage intake and gastric cancer incidence”, Gastro Hep Advances (2026)

items.author: secretsofuniverse
items.text:
🌕 Venus may have once had a moon, and then destroyed it.

Today, Venus has no natural satellite. That has always been strange, because Venus is so similar to Earth in size, mass and rocky composition.

Earth has a large Moon.

Venus has nothing.

A new study tested whether Venus could have formed a moon after a giant impact, only to lose it later through tides.

The team modeled a gravitational tug-of-war between Venus, the Sun and a hypothetical moon over billions of years.

The result was surprisingly brutal.

In many scenarios, the moon first moved outward, much like our Moon is slowly drifting away from Earth today.

But as the moon drained Venus’ spin, the balance changed.

Its orbit could reverse, forcing the moon to spiral back inward toward the planet.

Once it crossed Venus’ Roche limit, the moon would be torn apart by gravity, briefly forming a ring before much of the debris rained down onto Venus.

A heavier moon would not necessarily survive longer.

It could actually speed up its own destruction by slowing Venus faster.

This does not prove Venus had a moon.

But it shows that if it did, Venus may have swallowed the evidence long ago.

📄 RESEARCH PAPER
📌 Kane et al., “Tidal Demise: The Evolution and Fate of a Hypothetical Venus Moon”, The Astrophysical Journal, accepted (2026)

items.author: TornadoChasing
items.text:
Being my 19th birthday, I decided to skip my college classes for the day. My dad had called me that morning and told me about the first plane. 

At the time, we had no idea it was an attack and sort of joked "how does some idiot crash into a building that large." We didn't know it was a full size jet. We thought it was a small personal plane.

Turned on the TV to check the news just as plane two hit....the room went silent. This was no longer an accident...and the entire demeanor changed. 

Dad called me back and said "I think you should stay home from school." (lol he didn't know his degenerate son already planned to skip it.)

One by one, all the other TV stations stopped their programing for the day. Something unheard of back in the day. Remember, this is pre-everything about the modern internet era. No fb, no X, no YT, no phone apps, NONE of the crap we all use today. Just AIM, land lines and clunky Nokia cell phones with a snake game when text messages cost 10 cents each.

From there on, 24/7 news coverage. Staring at the TV. My family attempted a sad Bday dinner at a local restaurant but it was nothing but silence staring at the TV letting the food get cold. 

The day just got worse and worse as it evolved. The Pentagon, UA flight 93 and the heroes who forced the plane to not reach its likely target (the white house.)

Living next to Midway Airport in Chicago, and used to the noisy traffic of planes constantly taking off and landing, an eery silence fell over the hood once the FAA grounded all flights. It was unnatural, it was creepy. 

Until the fighter jets showed up. Is this really happening??

Everything changed that day. Terrorism was sort of just a bla bla thing we knew existed but still felt immune to. That day it became really real. We never felt more vulnerable.

Then, in the days after, we were never more united. It sucks it takes something like that to bring unity....but the unity was beautiful. Something I wish would happen again (minus the tragedy obviously) but probably never will.

Those too young to remember or born after will never understand such a level of unity, nor how the world changed. I wish they could experience what real unity feels like, and hope they never have to live through a day like that.  

For those who lived it, Never Forget. For those who didn't, try to understand.

TIMES ARE CHANGING: We all know the days are getting shorter this time of year. But it's so much deeper than that. 

The path our Sun takes in the sky is dramatically changing. On the summer solstice, the Sun climbs as high as 70° in the sky, eventually setting in on the northwest horizon. Today, the peak angle is only 51° with the Sun setting closer to due west. When winter arrives, the Sun rises only 23° and sets very early in the west-southwestern sky. This is the byproduct of Earth's axial tilt. Pay attention the next time your watch a sunset. Make a mental note of where on the horizon it sets. You'll notice it slowly changing locations each evening!

items.author: secretsofuniverse
items.text:
💨 Webb has caught a giant planet leaking helium into space.

The planet is WASP-107b, a strange super-puff world about 212 light-years away in the constellation Virgo.

It is almost the size of Jupiter, but has only about 12% of Jupiter’s mass.

That makes it so low-density that astronomers often compare it to cotton candy.

Using JWST’s NIRISS instrument, scientists watched starlight pass through the planet’s extended atmosphere.

They found helium absorption beginning about 1.5 hours before the planet even started crossing its star.

That means the gas is not just sitting close to the planet.

It is streaming far into space.

Models show helium flowing both ahead of and behind WASP-107b, forming long tails that stretch up to nearly 10 times the planet’s radius.

The planet orbits extremely close to its star, where radiation and stellar wind can strip away its outer atmosphere.

Webb also confirmed water in the atmosphere and found signs of strong chemical mixing.

Together, the results suggest WASP-107b may have formed farther out, then migrated inward, where its atmosphere became inflated and began escaping.

This is not just a planet with a leaky sky.

It is a world being reshaped by its star in real time.

📄 RESEARCH PAPER
📌 Krishnamurthy et al., “Continuous helium absorption from both the leading and trailing tails of WASP-107 b”, Nature Astronomy (2026)

🌗 Astronomers have found a dead star with two completely different faces.

The object is a white dwarf called ZTF J203349.8+322901.1, about 1,300 light-years away in Cygnus.

White dwarfs are the dense leftover cores of stars like the Sun. They pack roughly a star’s worth of mass into a body about the size of Earth.

But this one is unlike any white dwarf seen before.

As it spins once every 15 minutes, its spectrum changes dramatically.

When one side faces Earth, astronomers see hydrogen. When the other side rotates into view, they see helium.

That is why the team nicknamed it Janus, after the two-faced Roman god of transition.

The star is probably caught during a rare phase in white dwarf evolution, when its outer atmosphere is changing from hydrogen-dominated to helium-dominated as it cools.

Normally, this transition should happen across the whole star.

But Janus seems split in half.

The leading idea is that a weak magnetic field may be controlling how material mixes across its surface, allowing helium to rise on one side while hydrogen remains on the other.

It is a strange glimpse of a dying star mid-transformation.

A cosmic corpse with two faces, turning every 15 minutes.

📄 RESEARCH PAPER
📌 Caiazzo et al., “A rotating white dwarf shows different compositions on its opposite faces”, Nature (2023)
